script.title: How to make a budget (step by step, in one evening)
script.hook: Most people don't fail at budgeting because they're bad with money. They fail because the budget they picked asks for fifty small decisions a day, and nobody has the energy for that after work. Tonight we'll build one that asks for one decision a month and a twenty-minute check-in once a week. You'll need about an hour, your last two months of bank and card statements, and something to write on. By the end you'll have four numbers that cover every dollar you earn, and one of them is the only number you'll think about day to day. We'll use a made-up person, Sam, so you can see real math.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Most people don't fail at budgeting because they're bad with money. You'll need about an hour, your last two months of bank and card statements, and something to write on. By the end you'll have four numbers that cover every dollar you earn, and one of them is the only number you'll think about day to day. We'll use a made-up person, Sam, so you can see real math.

segments.heading: Gather your numbers
segments.narration: Before any planning, collect facts. Download two months of statements for every checking account and credit card. Two months matters, because one month can be unusual. Open them side by side and get a highlighter or a spreadsheet ready. You're looking for three things: what actually landed in your account from work, what repeated every month, and what showed up once but will clearly happen again, like a car registration or a friend's wedding. Don't judge anything yet. Judging slows you down and makes people quit in the first ten minutes. Tonight you're a researcher, not a critic.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two neat stacks of paper with a highlighter shape resting on top. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 1: true take-home
segments.narration: Your budget starts with money that actually arrives, not your salary. Find your normal paychecks and convert them to a monthly figure. Paid every two weeks? Multiply one paycheck by twenty-six, then divide by twelve. Paid weekly? Multiply by fifty-two, divide by twelve. Twice a month? Just double it. Sam is paid every two weeks, $1,400 each time. Fourteen hundred times twenty-six is $36,400, divided by twelve is about $3,033. We'll round down to $3,000 to keep a little slack. If your income varies, use your lowest normal month from the last six, and treat anything above that as a bonus to assign later.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a paycheck envelope feeding a small calculator made of simple shapes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 2: Bills
segments.narration: Line one is Bills: every cost that repeats each month at roughly the same amount. Rent, power, internet, phone, car insurance, transit, minimum payments on every debt, and subscriptions. Go line by line through the statements. For bills that change with the seasons, like heating, use a slightly high average so winter doesn't surprise you. Sam's list comes to $1,650: rent $1,150, utilities and internet $140, phone $45, car insurance $110, gas and transit $105, a student loan minimum of $100. If your Bills line is above about sixty percent of take-home, the biggest wins will come from the bills themselves, not from skipping coffee.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a shelf with a house, lightbulb, phone and car icon in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 3: Funds
segments.narration: Line two is Funds, short for sinking funds. These are the costs that aren't monthly but always come: car repairs, gifts, medical copays, annual renewals, travel, new shoes. They're the real reason most budgets break, because they get treated as emergencies when they were completely predictable. Look back over twelve months, estimate a yearly amount for each, and divide by twelve. Sam sets aside $100 for car costs, $60 for gifts, $40 for medical and $50 for travel. That's $250 a month. The money sits in savings until the cost arrives, and then it's spent without any guilt, because that's exactly what it was for.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a row of small ribbon-tied jars with car, gift and plane icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 4: Goals
segments.narration: Line three is Goals, and it gets paid first, not from whatever is left over. Goals can be a starter emergency fund, extra payments on high-interest debt, or investing for retirement. Pick an amount that's meaningful but not painful, because you can raise it at any monthly reset. Sam chooses $300: $200 toward a starter emergency fund until it reaches one month of essentials, and $100 extra on a credit card. If you have an employer retirement match, the contribution comes out of your paycheck before it ever reaches you, so it won't appear here, but make sure you're getting it. That match is part of your pay.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a plant growing out of a savings jar with a small upward arrow. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 5: your weekly number
segments.narration: Line four is the one you'll actually live with. Take home pay, minus Bills, minus Funds, minus Goals. For Sam that's $3,000 minus $1,650, minus $250, minus $300, which leaves $800 a month. To turn that into a weekly number, multiply by twelve and divide by fifty-two. That's about $184 a week. Groceries, eating out, coffee, fun, a birthday drink, a random lamp: all of it comes out of $184. There are no categories inside it to police. Sam decides the trade-offs at the checkout, which is where those decisions really happen anyway. When the week's money is gone, the week is done.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a single wallet resting on a small seven-day calendar strip. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 6: make it automatic
segments.narration: A plan you have to remember is a plan you'll forget. Set it up so the first three lines run without you. Bills and Goals leave checking automatically the day after payday. Funds go to a separate savings account, ideally one that earns a decent rate and is insured, so the money isn't sitting idle. The weekly number moves into a spending account, or onto one card you pay in full every month. Sam sets two automatic transfers per paycheck and turns on autopay for every bill. From now on, the only balance Sam needs to check is the spending one, and it only has to last until Sunday.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a simple gear system moving coins from one jar into three others. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Step 7: the first check-in
segments.narration: Put a recurring twenty-minute event in your calendar for the same evening every week. At the first one, do five things. Write down how much of last week's number you spent. If there's money left, roll it into this week or send it to a goal. If you went over, take it from this week. Look three weeks ahead for anything unusual and check the right fund can cover it. Then confirm this week's number and close the laptop. That's the entire tracking system: one number a week, not every coffee. Most check-ins take ten minutes once the habit is set, sometimes less.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes on a sofa with a timer, a mug and a closed laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When week one goes wrong
segments.narration: It will, a little, and that's useful information, not failure. Maybe Sam spends $230 in the first week because of a friend's birthday dinner. The fix isn't guilt or a new budget. Sam takes the extra $46 out of next week, so week two is $138, and makes a note. If it keeps happening, the plan is wrong, not Sam. At the monthly reset, Sam can move money from Goals to the weekly number for a month, or find a bill to cut. Never rewrite the plan mid-week, in the heat of a bad day. Write it down and decide at the monthly reset, when you're calm.
segments.on_screen_text: Over? Take it from next week.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small stumble on a path with the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes getting back up and smiling. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The monthly reset
segments.narration: Once a month, give the whole plan twenty minutes. Check whether each bill is still accurate, whether the funds are on track for what's coming, and whether the weekly number felt livable. Adjust one or two things, not everything. This is where you raise a goal after a raise, add a new fund for a holiday trip, or cancel a subscription you noticed you never use. Over a few months, the numbers stop being guesses and start being yours. Sam's first reset moves $20 from gifts to car costs, because a tire looks worn. That's the system working: small adjustments, made calmly, in advance.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Here's the whole evening in one breath. Find your true take-home pay. List Bills. Plan Funds for the costs that always come. Pay Goals first. Whatever's left becomes your weekly number. Automate the first three lines, then run a twenty-minute check-in every week and a twenty-minute reset every month. If you want this ready-made, our guide and spreadsheet, The 20-Minute Budget, walks through the same steps and does the weekly math for you. It's our own product and the link is in the bio. Either way, you can build it tonight with a notepad. Pick the evening, and put it on the calendar now.

script.title: High-yield savings accounts, explained properly
script.hook: If your savings live at the same bank as your checking account, there's a decent chance they're earning almost nothing. That isn't a scam, exactly. It's just that many big banks don't need to compete for your savings, so they don't. High-yield savings accounts exist because other banks do want your deposits, and they pay for them. In this video we'll cover why the rates are different, what the numbers actually look like, how to tell if an account is safe, the fees and limits to check, how interest gets taxed, and what money belongs in one. Then a five-minute way to pick one.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If your savings live at the same bank as your checking account, there's a decent chance they're earning almost nothing. That isn't a scam, exactly. It's just that many big banks don't need to compete for your savings, so they don't. High-yield savings accounts exist because other banks do want your deposits, and they pay for them. In this video we'll cover why the rates are different, what the numbers actually look like, how to tell if an account is safe, the fees and limits to check, how interest gets taxed, and what money belongs in one. Then a five-minute way to pick one.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes peeking into a nearly empty jar inside a big quiet bank lobby. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why rates differ
segments.narration: A high-yield savings account is just a savings account with a higher interest rate. Most are at online banks or online divisions of traditional banks. Without a big branch network to pay for, they can pass more of their earnings to depositors. They also use higher rates to attract customers, the same way a store runs a sale. The rate is variable, meaning the bank can change it at any time, and rates across the whole market tend to rise and fall with the Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions. So a high-yield account isn't a locked deal. It's a better default, which you check in on once in a while.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small modern building and a large columned building, coins flowing faster from the small one. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The numbers
segments.narration: Let's make it concrete with an emergency fund of $6,000. At a rate of 0.01% APY, which some large banks still pay on basic savings, that earns about sixty cents a year. At an illustrative 3.5% APY, the same $6,000 earns roughly $210 in a year, if the rate stays there. Add $200 a month for a year at that rate and you'd put in $2,400 and earn about forty dollars of interest on top. None of this will make you rich, and it isn't meant to. The point is that money you're keeping safe anyway shouldn't lose ground for no reason.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. two jars, one with a single coin and one with a modest stack, on a balance scale. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: APY and compounding
segments.narration: The number to compare is APY, the annual percentage yield. It includes compounding, which means the interest you earn starts earning interest too. Most savings accounts compound daily or monthly and pay interest monthly. With savings rates, compounding makes only a small difference in one year, so don't overthink daily versus monthly. Compare APY to APY. Be careful with headlines that show a high rate with an asterisk. It might be a promotional rate for a few months, or it might only apply up to a certain balance, or require a direct deposit. The fine print will say. If an offer needs a lot of conditions, it may not be worth the effort.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a snowball rolling gently and growing slightly bigger. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Is it safe?
segments.narration: Safety comes from deposit insurance, not from the app's design. At a bank, look for FDIC insurance, which covers deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, if the bank fails. At a credit union, the equivalent is NCUA insurance. Some savings apps aren't banks at all. They partner with a bank that holds your money. In that case, the insurance covers the partner bank failing, not the app company running into trouble. You can look up any bank in the FDIC's BankFind tool in about a minute. If you can't figure out where your money actually sits, that's your answer: pick a different account.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a sturdy umbrella over a jar, with a small magnifying glass beside it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Fees and limits
segments.narration: A good high-yield account shouldn't charge a monthly maintenance fee or require a large minimum balance to earn its rate. Check anyway. Then look at how money gets out. Most connect to your checking account through an electronic transfer that usually takes one to three business days. That's a feature for an emergency fund, a small speed bump that stops casual spending, but plan around it. Some banks also limit how many withdrawals or transfers you can make per month. A federal rule used to cap certain savings withdrawals at six per month; that requirement was dropped in 2020, but some banks still set their own limits.
segments.on_screen_text: No fees. Know the transfer time.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small bridge with a coin crossing slowly between two jars, a clock above it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxes on interest
segments.narration: Interest from a savings account is taxable income. If you earn ten dollars or more in a year, the bank usually sends a form 1099-INT, and you report it on your tax return. At the amounts most people in their twenties hold, this is small, but it's worth knowing so it isn't a surprise. It's taxed at your ordinary income tax rate, unlike some investments that get special treatment. Treasury bills are one alternative for short-term money that's exempt from state income tax, which can matter in high-tax states. For most people starting out, though, the simplicity of a savings account wins.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a small envelope with a coin, next to a simple calculator. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What belongs in one
segments.narration: A high-yield savings account is a great home for three kinds of money. First, your emergency fund, money you might need tomorrow without warning. Second, sinking funds, the money you're setting aside for car repairs, gifts and annual bills. Third, short-term goals within a couple of years, like a move, a deposit on an apartment, or a trip. Keeping these separate from checking makes them less tempting to spend. Some people open several accounts, or use a bank that lets you create labeled sub-accounts, so each pot has a name. Seeing 'car repairs' with $340 in it is weirdly calming when the check engine light comes on.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. three labeled-by-color jars on a shelf: umbrella, ribbon, plane. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What doesn't
segments.narration: Long-term money, especially for retirement, generally shouldn't live in savings for decades. Over long periods, cash has often struggled to keep up with inflation, while diversified investments have historically grown faster, with real ups and downs. That money belongs in a retirement account and low-cost investments. The opposite mistake also happens: investing your emergency fund to chase a higher return. If the market drops at the same time you lose your job, you'd be selling at the worst moment. So the rule is simple. Money for the next year or two goes in savings. Money for decades goes into investments. Don't swap them.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. a timeline with a jar on the left and a growing tree on the right. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Choose in 5 minutes
segments.narration: Here's the quick way. One: confirm FDIC or NCUA insurance, and the partner bank if it's an app. Two: compare the current APY across two or three options, not just the one in an ad. Three: check there's no monthly fee and no minimum to earn the rate. Four: check transfer time and any monthly limits. Five: make sure it links easily to your checking account and that you can close it online. Then open it, move your emergency fund, and set up an automatic transfer every payday. You don't need the single highest rate in the country. You need a good rate at a safe bank that you'll actually use.
segments.visual_prompt: Warm flat vector illustration, muted greens and cream with a mustard accent, simple shapes. the small round green piggy bank mascot with big eyes ticking five checkboxes on a clipboard. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: A high-yield savings account is a regular insured savings account with a better, variable rate. The rate difference is mostly about how much the bank wants deposits, not about extra risk, as long as it's insured. Use it for emergency money, sinking funds and short-term goals. Keep long-term money invested. Compare by APY, check fees, transfers and limits, and remember interest is taxable.
